title: Securities Markets Foundation
blurb: The entry-level certification on how Indian securities markets work, from shares and IPOs to funds, derivatives and financial planning.

units.title: Understanding securities markets and performance
units.overview: Securities markets move savings of households into the investments of companies and governments. This chapter explains why markets exist, who takes part, and who keeps them honest.
focus: Primary versus secondary market.
Money market versus capital market.
Roles of SEBI, RBI and other regulators.
facts: Securities market
The securities market is where securities such as shares, bonds and units are issued and traded, channelling savings into productive investment.
A company raises money by selling shares to the public, and investors later trade those shares.
The securities market deals only in physical goods.
Primary market
The primary market is where new securities are issued for the first time and the issuer receives the money.
A company launches an IPO and receives funds from investors.
Investors trade with each other in the primary market.
Secondary market
The secondary market is where existing securities are bought and sold among investors, usually on a stock exchange, providing liquidity.
An investor sells shares she bought last year to another investor on an exchange.
The issuing company receives the money when shares trade in the secondary market.
Money market
The money market deals in short-term debt instruments with a maturity of up to one year, such as treasury bills and commercial paper.
A company raises funds for 90 days by issuing a short-term instrument.
The money market deals in securities of 10 years or more.
Capital market
The capital market deals in long-term securities such as equity shares and bonds with maturities beyond one year.
A company issues 10-year bonds to fund a new factory.
The capital market deals only in securities of less than one year.
SEBI
The Securities and Exchange Board of India regulates the securities market, protects investors and promotes market development.
A broker that violates trading rules is penalised by the market regulator.
SEBI sets the repo rate.
Market participants
Participants include issuers, investors, brokers, depositories, clearing corporations, merchant bankers, mutual funds and regulators.
An investor buys through a broker, with units held at a depository and trades settled by a clearing corporation.
The only participants in the securities market are investors and issuers.
Financial intermediation
Financial intermediaries connect savers and borrowers and add value through pooling, risk management and information.
A bank takes deposits from savers and lends to borrowers.
Intermediaries add no value to the financial system.
Market efficiency
An efficient market reflects available information in prices quickly, making it hard to consistently earn abnormal returns.
Share prices adjust within seconds of a company announcing results.
In an efficient market prices never move.
Market performance indicators
Indices, market capitalisation, turnover and the number of investors are used to assess how a market is performing.
An analyst reviews the Sensex and daily turnover to judge market activity.
Market performance is measured only by the price of one share.

units.title: Securities: types, features and concepts
units.overview: Equity, preference shares, bonds, government securities and money market instruments all have different rights and risks. This is the biggest topic and most questions are definition or comparison based.
focus: Equity versus preference shares.
Bonds, debentures, G-secs, T-bills, CP and CD.
Corporate actions: dividend, bonus, split, rights, buyback.
Credit ratings and key valuation ratios.
visuals: Priority over equity for dividend and capital
facts: Equity share
An equity share represents ownership in a company. Holders are residual owners who vote, receive dividends when declared, and share in the profits and losses.
An investor buying shares in a listed company becomes a part-owner.
Equity shareholders are guaranteed a fixed dividend.
Preference share
A preference share carries a preferential right to a fixed dividend and to repayment of capital ahead of equity holders on winding up, usually with no voting rights.
A holder is paid a fixed rate of dividend before any dividend goes to equity holders.
Preference shareholders always have full voting rights.
Face value
Face value is the nominal value of a security stated on the certificate; dividends are declared as a percentage of it.
A share has a face value of ₹10 while its market price is ₹450.
Face value is the price at which the share trades in the market.
Market capitalisation
Market capitalisation equals the share price multiplied by the number of shares outstanding, and shows the market value of a company's equity.
A company with 10 crore shares priced at ₹200 is valued at ₹2,000 crore.
Market capitalisation equals the company's total debt.
Dividend
A dividend is a distribution of part of a company's profits to its shareholders, declared by the board and approved by shareholders.
A company pays ₹5 per share to every holder on the record date.
A company must pay a dividend every year.
Bonus shares
Bonus shares are free additional shares given to existing shareholders in a ratio from the company's reserves; the share price adjusts and total value is unchanged.
A holder with 100 shares receives 100 more in a 1:1 bonus, while the price roughly halves.
Bonus shares increase the investor's wealth immediately.
Stock split
A stock split divides each share into more shares of lower face value, increasing the number of shares while leaving market capitalisation unchanged.
A ₹10 face value share is split into two shares of ₹5 each.
A stock split increases the company's market capitalisation.
Rights issue
A rights issue offers existing shareholders the right to buy additional shares in proportion to their holding, usually at a discount.
A company offers current holders one new share for every four held at a set price.
A rights issue is open to the general public.
Buyback
In a buyback, a company repurchases its own shares from shareholders, reducing the number of shares outstanding.
A company buys back shares through a tender offer, and the share count falls.
A buyback increases the number of shares outstanding.
Bond
A bond is a debt instrument in which the issuer promises to pay periodic interest (coupon) and repay the principal at maturity.
An investor lends to a company and receives interest every six months and principal at the end.
A bond makes the holder an owner of the company.
Debenture
A debenture is a long-term debt instrument issued by a company, which can be secured or unsecured and may be convertible into shares.
A company raises money by issuing a convertible debt instrument.
A debenture is an equity instrument.
Government security (G-sec)
A G-sec is a debt instrument issued by the central or a state government, considered to have negligible credit risk.
The central government borrows by issuing a 10-year security.
G-secs carry the highest credit risk in the market.
Treasury bill
A treasury bill is a short-term government money-market instrument issued at a discount and redeemed at face value, with tenors of 91, 182 and 364 days.
The government issues a 91-day instrument at ₹98 that is redeemed at ₹100.
Treasury bills pay periodic coupons.
Commercial paper
Commercial paper is an unsecured, short-term money-market instrument issued by companies at a discount to meet working-capital needs.
A highly rated company raises funds for three months without collateral.
Commercial paper is a long-term secured bond.
Certificate of deposit
A certificate of deposit is a negotiable money-market instrument issued by banks and financial institutions against funds deposited for a fixed period.
A bank issues a negotiable paper against a large deposit for six months.
A certificate of deposit is issued by the government.
Coupon rate
The coupon rate is the fixed percentage of face value that a bond pays as interest each year.
A bond of ₹1,000 face value with a 8% coupon pays ₹80 a year.
The coupon rate changes with the bond's market price.
Yield
Yield is the return an investor earns on a security, shown as a percentage of the price paid. It moves inversely to bond prices.
When a bond's price rises, the yield for a new buyer falls.
Bond yields rise when bond prices rise.
Credit rating
A credit rating is an independent agency's opinion on the issuer's ability to repay debt on time. Higher ratings mean lower risk.
An issuer rated AAA is seen as safer than one rated BBB.
A credit rating guarantees that the issuer will not default.
Convertible security
A convertible security can be converted into equity shares at a specified ratio and time, at the holder's or issuer's option.
A debenture holder exchanges the debenture for shares as per pre-set terms.
A convertible security can never be converted into shares.
Depository receipt
A depository receipt represents shares of a company held by a depository in another country, such as ADRs and GDRs, and allows foreign trading of the underlying shares.
An Indian company's shares are traded abroad through receipts issued against them.
A depository receipt is issued only for bonds.
Price-to-earnings ratio
The P/E ratio is the market price per share divided by earnings per share. It shows how much investors pay for each rupee of earnings.
A share priced at ₹200 with EPS of ₹10 has a ratio of 20.
P/E is the share price divided by its face value.
Earnings per share
EPS is a company's profit after tax divided by the number of shares outstanding.
A company with ₹100 crore profit and 10 crore shares has an EPS of ₹10.
EPS is the dividend paid per share.
REIT and InvIT
REITs and InvITs are trusts that pool money to invest in income-generating real estate and infrastructure and distribute most income to unit holders.
An investor buys units of a trust that owns rented office buildings.
REITs invest only in shares of listed companies.
Warrants
A warrant gives the holder the right to buy a company's shares at a fixed price within a specified period.
An investor holds a right to buy shares at ₹100 for the next three years.
A warrant obliges the holder to buy shares.
Gilt versus corporate bond
Government securities carry negligible credit risk, while corporate bonds carry credit risk and pay a higher yield for it.
A saver compares a government bond with a corporate bond offering a higher rate.
Corporate bonds are safer than government securities.

units.title: Primary markets
units.overview: How companies raise money from the public: IPOs, FPOs, rights, QIPs and private placements. The mechanics of book building, categories of investors, and listing are tested closely.
focus: IPO process and documents.
Book building, price band and cut-off price.
Investor categories and reservation.
Other routes: rights, QIP, preferential, OFS.
facts: Initial Public Offer (IPO)
An IPO is the first offer of shares by an unlisted company to the public, after which the company's shares are listed on an exchange.
A private company sells shares to the public for the first time.
An IPO is the sale of already listed shares between investors.
Follow-on Public Offer (FPO)
An FPO is an offer of additional shares to the public by a company that is already listed.
A listed company raises more capital by offering new shares to the public.
An FPO is the first listing of a company.
Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP)
The DRHP is the draft offer document filed with SEBI for observations before an IPO, without final price details.
A company files its draft offer document through a merchant banker before launching its issue.
The DRHP is the final document circulated after listing.
Book building
In book building, the price is discovered through bids within a price band, and the issue price is fixed after the bidding closes based on demand.
Investors bid within a price band and the final price is decided after the issue closes.
In book building the price is fixed by the regulator.
Price band
The price band is the range between the floor and the cap price within which investors can bid in a book-built issue. The cap should not exceed 120% of the floor.
An IPO sets a range of ₹200 to ₹210 for bids.
Investors can bid at any price above the floor with no cap.
Cut-off price
Retail investors can bid at the cut-off price, which means they accept whatever final price is decided within the band.
A retail investor chooses to accept the final price fixed by the issuer.
The cut-off price is the lowest price in the band.
Anchor investors
Anchor investors are qualified institutional investors who are allotted shares before the issue opens, subject to a lock-in, to build confidence.
Institutions are allotted a portion a day before the IPO opens.
Anchor investors are retail individuals.
Retail individual investor
A retail individual investor is one who bids for shares worth up to ₹2 lakh in an issue.
A person applies for ₹1.5 lakh worth of shares in an IPO.
A retail investor can apply for any amount in the retail quota.
Qualified institutional buyer
QIBs are institutions such as mutual funds, banks, insurers and foreign portfolio investors that are considered financially sophisticated.
A mutual fund bids in the institutional category of an IPO.
QIBs are individuals applying for ₹1 lakh.
Minimum subscription
An issue must receive at least 90% subscription of the issue size; otherwise application money is refunded.
An IPO that gets only half the required subscription fails and money is returned.
An IPO can proceed with 10% subscription.
Allotment and listing timeline
Shares are allotted and listed within three working days of the closure of the issue, and unsuccessful applicants are refunded.
The issue closes on Monday and shares list within a few working days.
Listing takes place a month after closing.
ASBA
Application Supported by Blocked Amount means the application money stays blocked in the investor's bank account until allotment, and is debited only for allotted shares.
An investor's funds are blocked, not transferred, while applying to an IPO.
ASBA debits the full amount immediately and refunds later.
Merchant banker
A merchant banker, also called the book running lead manager, manages the issue process, prepares offer documents and ensures regulatory compliance.
A SEBI-registered firm manages the whole IPO process for a company.
A merchant banker buys the shares as a retail investor.
Underwriter
An underwriter agrees to buy the unsubscribed portion of an issue, giving the issuer certainty of raising funds.
A firm promises to take up the shares not bought by the public.
An underwriter guarantees profit to investors.
Registrar to the issue
The registrar to an issue processes applications, finalises allotment, issues refunds and maintains the shareholder records.
An agency handles the allotment and refund process for an IPO.
The registrar fixes the issue price.
Offer for Sale (OFS)
In an OFS, existing shareholders such as promoters sell their shares to the public through the exchange, and the company receives no money.
A promoter sells part of his stake through a stock exchange window.
An OFS brings new capital into the company.
Qualified Institutions Placement (QIP)
A QIP is a route for listed companies to raise capital by issuing shares or convertibles only to qualified institutional buyers.
A listed company issues new shares to institutions at a price near the market.
A QIP is open to retail investors.
Preferential allotment
A preferential allotment is the issue of shares to a select group of investors at a negotiated price, subject to regulatory pricing rules.
A company issues shares to a chosen strategic investor.
A preferential allotment is offered to all shareholders pro rata.
Private placement
In a private placement, securities are offered to a limited number of identified investors rather than the general public.
A company raises debt from a handful of institutions.
A private placement is a public issue.
Promoter lock-in
Promoters' minimum contribution of 20% of the post-issue capital is locked in for 18 months after listing, to show their commitment.
Promoters cannot sell their minimum holding for a period after the listing.
Promoters can sell all their shares on listing day.
SME platform
SME platforms on exchanges allow small and medium enterprises to list with simpler rules but with larger minimum application sizes and higher risk.
A small company raises capital on a dedicated exchange segment.
SME platform issues are the same as main-board IPOs.
Red Herring Prospectus
The RHP is the offer document filed with the registrar before the issue opens; it contains issue details but the final price may not be fixed.
A company files a document with the registrar before the issue opens.
The RHP is filed after the allotment.

units.title: Secondary markets
units.overview: Where shares trade every day. This chapter covers exchanges, brokers, orders, indices, settlement, the depository system and the safeguards that protect the market.
focus: Stock exchanges, trading hours and settlement.
Order types and price bands.
Depositories and demat.
Indices and circuit breakers.
facts: Stock exchange
A stock exchange is a regulated marketplace where securities are listed and traded, such as the BSE and the NSE.
Buyers and sellers trade listed shares on a regulated electronic platform.
A stock exchange sets the company's profit.
Trading hours
Equity trading on Indian exchanges runs from 9:15 am to 3:30 pm on business days, with a pre-open session from 9:00 am to 9:15 am.
An investor places an order at 9:20 am during the regular session.
Equity markets trade 24 hours a day.
Settlement cycle
Equity trades are settled on a T+1 basis, which means securities and funds are exchanged one working day after the trade.
A share bought on Monday is delivered to the buyer's account on Tuesday.
Equity trades settle on T+5.
Stockbroker
A stockbroker is a SEBI-registered member of an exchange who executes trades for clients and earns brokerage.
An investor places her order through a registered intermediary who is an exchange member.
Investors can trade directly on the exchange without a member.
Demat account
A demat account holds securities in electronic form and is opened with a depository participant.
An investor holds her shares electronically rather than as paper certificates.
A demat account holds only physical share certificates.
Depository
A depository holds securities in electronic form and enables transfer of ownership through book entries. India has two: NSDL and CDSL.
A institution keeps electronic records of who owns which shares.
India has five depositories.
Depository participant (DP)
A DP is an agent of the depository, such as a bank or broker, through which investors open demat accounts and deal with the depository.
An investor opens a demat account through her bank, which acts as the link to the depository.
A DP is the stock exchange itself.
Clearing corporation
A clearing corporation acts as the counterparty to every trade, guarantees settlement and manages risk, ensuring that trades are completed.
The entity that guarantees that both sides of a trade will be honoured settles the trade.
A clearing corporation sets share prices.
Market order
A market order is an instruction to buy or sell immediately at the best available price in the market.
An investor wants to buy at once and accepts the prevailing price.
A market order fixes the price in advance.
Limit order
A limit order is an instruction to buy or sell at a specified price or better; it may not be executed if the market does not reach that price.
An investor will buy only at ₹100 or lower.
A limit order is always executed immediately.
Stop-loss order
A stop-loss order becomes active when the price reaches a trigger level and is used to limit losses on a position.
A holder places an order to sell if the price falls to ₹90.
A stop-loss order guarantees profit.
Circuit filter
A circuit filter is a price band that limits how much a stock's price can move in a day, to curb excessive volatility.
A stock cannot rise more than 10% in a day because of its price band.
Circuit filters stop trading for the whole year.
Index circuit breaker
Index-based circuit breakers halt trading across the market when the index moves by 10%, 15% or 20% within a day.
The market is halted when the benchmark index falls 10%.
Index circuit breakers apply only to single stocks.
Sensex
The Sensex is the benchmark index of the BSE, comprising 30 large and actively traded stocks, calculated on a free-float market-cap basis.
An index of 30 leading companies on the Bombay exchange.
The Sensex has 50 stocks.
Nifty 50
The Nifty 50 is the benchmark index of the NSE, made of 50 large companies and calculated on a free-float market-cap basis.
An index of 50 leading companies on the National exchange.
The Nifty 50 tracks the debt market.
Free-float market capitalisation
Free-float market cap counts only the shares available for public trading, excluding promoter and locked-in holdings.
An index weights a company by shares that the public can actually trade.
Free-float market cap includes all shares, including promoters'.
Bid and ask
The bid is the highest price a buyer is willing to pay, and the ask is the lowest price a seller will accept; the gap is the spread.
A stock shows buyers at ₹99.90 and sellers at ₹100.10.
The bid is always higher than the ask.
Liquidity in markets
A liquid market allows securities to be bought and sold quickly with little effect on price, shown by tight spreads and high volumes.
A heavily traded stock can be sold in seconds at a small spread.
A liquid stock is hard to sell.
Short selling
Short selling means selling a security you do not own, planning to buy it back later at a lower price; deliveries are managed through securities lending and borrowing.
A trader sells first, expecting the price to fall, and buys back later.
Short selling profits when the price rises.
Securities Transaction Tax
STT is a tax levied on transactions in listed securities on the exchange, such as on the value of delivery-based sale and purchase.
A small tax is charged on each trade executed on the exchange.
STT is a tax on listing a company.
Margin trading
Margin trading means buying securities with borrowed funds, with the investor putting up only a part of the value as margin.
An investor buys shares worth ₹1 lakh by depositing ₹25,000 and borrowing the rest.
Margin trading removes risk of loss.
Investor Protection Fund
Exchanges maintain funds to compensate investors in case of defaults by members, within limits set by the regulator.
An investor is compensated from an exchange fund when a broker defaults.
The fund guarantees profit on trades.
Surveillance
Exchanges monitor trading to detect price manipulation, insider trading and unusual activity, and use measures like surveillance frameworks.
An exchange flags a stock whose price rises abnormally on low volumes.
Exchanges do not monitor trades.
Insider trading
Insider trading is dealing in securities based on unpublished price-sensitive information, and it is prohibited by SEBI.
A director sells shares just before bad results are announced publicly.
Insider trading is legal if profits are small.
Call auction
In a call auction, orders are collected over a time window and matched at a single price, as in the pre-open session.
Orders gather between 9:00 and 9:08 am and the opening price is discovered together.
A call auction matches each order continuously one by one.

units.title: Mutual funds
units.overview: Mutual funds pool money from many investors. This chapter covers structure, NAV, scheme types, costs, SIP and what to read before investing.
focus: Structure of a mutual fund and its NAV.
Scheme types: equity, debt, hybrid, index, ETF.
SIP, expense ratio, exit load and riskometer.
How to choose a fund.
visuals: NAV = (Value of investments + other assets − liabilities) ÷ units outstanding
facts: Mutual fund
A mutual fund pools money from many investors and invests it in securities through professional managers, and each investor owns units in proportion.
A group of investors puts money together, and a team invests it for them.
A mutual fund guarantees returns.
NAV
The Net Asset Value is the per-unit value of a mutual fund scheme, calculated as total assets less liabilities divided by the units outstanding.
A scheme with ₹500 crore net assets and 10 crore units has a value of ₹50 per unit.
NAV is the price paid for a share on the exchange.
Asset Management Company
The AMC manages the mutual fund's schemes and investments and is appointed by the trustees.
A company runs the fund's portfolios and employs the fund managers.
The AMC owns the securities of the fund.
Open-ended fund
An open-ended fund allows investors to buy and sell units at NAV on any business day, with no fixed maturity.
An investor redeems on any working day at the day's NAV.
An open-ended fund can be redeemed only at maturity.
Closed-ended fund
A closed-ended fund has a fixed maturity and units are bought during the offer period and redeemed at maturity, or traded on an exchange.
A scheme with a three-year term takes money only at launch.
Closed-ended funds allow daily fresh purchases.
Equity fund
An equity fund invests mainly in shares and aims for long-term capital growth, with higher volatility.
A fund holds mostly shares to build wealth over many years.
An equity fund invests mainly in government bonds.
Debt fund
A debt fund invests in fixed-income securities such as bonds, treasury bills and money-market instruments, aiming for stable income.
A fund lends to governments and companies and earns interest.
A debt fund invests mostly in equity shares.
Hybrid fund
A hybrid fund invests in a mix of equity and debt to balance growth and stability.
A scheme keeps 65% in equity and the rest in debt.
A hybrid fund invests only in gold.
Index fund
An index fund passively replicates a market index such as the Nifty 50, holding its stocks in the same weights, with low cost.
A scheme tracks the Nifty 50 without trying to beat it.
An index fund tries to outperform the index through stock picking.
Exchange traded fund (ETF)
An ETF is a fund whose units trade on a stock exchange like a share and typically tracks an index or commodity.
An investor buys units of a fund through her demat account during market hours.
An ETF can only be bought directly from the AMC at NAV.
Liquid fund
A liquid fund invests in debt and money-market securities maturing within 91 days, for parking short-term surplus.
A company parks idle cash for a few weeks in a low-risk fund.
A liquid fund invests for 10 years in equity.
ELSS
An Equity Linked Savings Scheme is an equity fund with a three-year lock-in that qualifies for a tax deduction under the old tax regime.
An investor locks funds for three years to claim a deduction.
ELSS has a one-year lock-in.
SIP
A Systematic Investment Plan invests a fixed amount at regular intervals, building discipline and averaging the cost of purchase.
An investor puts ₹5,000 into a fund on the 5th of every month.
A SIP guarantees profit.
Rupee cost averaging
With a fixed amount invested regularly, more units are bought when NAV is low and fewer when it is high, reducing the average cost.
A SIP buys more units when prices fall.
Rupee cost averaging removes market risk.
Expense ratio
The expense ratio is the annual percentage of a scheme's assets charged for managing it. It is built into the NAV.
A fund with a 1% expense ratio retains ₹1 of every ₹100 each year for costs.
The expense ratio is a one-time charge when investing.
Exit load
Exit load is a fee charged when units are redeemed within a specified period, and it goes into the scheme.
An investor redeems after 6 months and 1% is deducted.
Exit load is charged on all purchases.
Direct plan
A direct plan is bought directly from the AMC without a distributor, so it has a lower expense ratio than a regular plan.
An investor buys on the fund house's website with no commission.
A direct plan has the highest expense ratio.
Riskometer
The riskometer is a gauge on each scheme showing its risk level on six levels from low to very high.
A scheme's cover shows a dial reading very high.
The riskometer shows past returns.
Growth and IDCW options
In the growth option, gains stay invested and reflect in NAV. In the IDCW option, the fund may pay out part of the gains periodically, reducing NAV.
An investor who wants regular cash payouts picks the income distribution option.
IDCW is a guaranteed dividend.
KYC for mutual funds
Investors must complete KYC with PAN and address proof before investing in mutual funds, and KYC is done once for the whole market.
A new investor completes identity verification before her first purchase.
KYC is not required for small investments.
Past performance
Past performance does not guarantee future returns; investors should look at consistency, risk and costs rather than a single year's number.
A fund topped the chart last year but may not repeat.
The best performer last year will stay best.
Fund manager
The fund manager is the person responsible for the investment decisions of a scheme, within its stated objective and asset allocation.
A professional decides which securities the scheme buys.
The fund manager guarantees returns.
Portfolio disclosure
Mutual funds publish portfolios and factsheets regularly so that investors can see their holdings.
An investor checks a scheme's top ten holdings in the monthly factsheet.
Portfolios are secret.
SEBI scheme categories
SEBI defines scheme categories and prevents AMCs from creating overlapping schemes with the same name and features, to make comparison easy.
A fund house cannot offer two identical large-cap funds.
AMCs can define their own categories freely.
Tax on equity funds
Equity-oriented fund gains are taxed as short-term if held up to 12 months and long-term beyond that, at rates set by law.
An investor sells units after 18 months and the gain is long-term.
Equity fund gains are tax free in all cases.

units.title: Derivatives markets
units.overview: Futures and options in simple terms: what they are, why people use them and the key vocabulary.
focus: Futures versus options.
Hedging, speculation, arbitrage.
Lot size, margin and expiry.
visuals: Buyer has a right; seller has an obligation
facts: Derivative
A derivative is a contract whose value is derived from an underlying asset such as a share, index, currency or commodity.
A contract whose value depends on the price of the Nifty 50.
A derivative has its own value, independent of any underlying.
Futures contract
A futures contract is an agreement to buy or sell an underlying at a fixed price on a future date, traded on an exchange with standard terms.
A trader agrees today to buy an index lot at a set price at month-end.
A futures contract is an option with no obligation.
Option contract
An option gives the buyer the right, but not the obligation, to buy or sell the underlying at a fixed price on or before expiry, in return for a premium.
An investor pays a fee to keep the right to buy a share at ₹100.
An option obliges the buyer to complete the trade.
Call option
A call option gives its buyer the right to buy the underlying at the strike price.
An investor expects prices to rise and buys the right to buy at ₹500.
A call option gives the right to sell.
Put option
A put option gives its buyer the right to sell the underlying at the strike price, and is used for protection or for gains when prices fall.
An investor holding a share buys the right to sell it at ₹90.
A put option gives the right to buy.
Strike price
The strike price is the fixed price at which the option holder can buy or sell the underlying.
An option allows the holder to buy at ₹2,500.
The strike price is the premium paid.
Premium
The premium is the price paid by the option buyer to the seller for the right granted.
The buyer pays ₹20 per unit for an option.
The premium is returned to the buyer at expiry.
Hedging
Hedging uses derivatives to reduce the risk of adverse price moves in an existing position.
A shareholder takes a position that offsets a possible fall in his holdings.
Hedging is aimed at maximising speculative profit.
Speculation
Speculation is taking a view on price direction and positions to profit from it, accepting the risk of loss.
A trader buys index futures expecting a rise over the next week.
Speculation is risk-free.
Arbitrage
Arbitrage involves buying and selling related instruments at the same time to profit from price differences, with little risk.
A trader buys a share in the cash market and sells its future at a higher price.
Arbitrage is a bet on market direction.
Lot size
The lot size is the fixed number of units in one derivatives contract, set by the exchange. Trading is in multiples of lots.
An index future trades in minimum quantities of 75 units.
Investors can trade any number of units in a futures contract.
Expiry
Expiry is the date on which a derivatives contract ceases to exist and is settled.
An options contract expires on a date fixed by the exchange.
Derivative contracts have no end date.
Margin in derivatives
Margin is the money a trader deposits with the broker as security for performing a futures or option-selling obligation.
A futures trader deposits a fraction of the contract value as security.
Margin is the full contract value.
Mark-to-market
Mark-to-market is the daily adjustment of futures positions to the day's settlement price, with gains and losses settled in cash.
A futures trader's account is credited or debited at the end of every day.

units.overview: Markets are a means to meet goals. This chapter links securities to planning: goals, risk profile, asset allocation, tax, insurance and avoiding frauds.

facts: Financial planning
Financial planning is the process of setting goals and arranging income, savings, investments, insurance and tax to meet them.
A family plans funds for a house, education and retirement.
Financial planning means only buying shares.
Financial goal
A financial goal is a specific need with an amount and a time frame, such as a child's education in 12 years.
A couple wants ₹30 lakh for education in ten years.
Goals need no amount or deadline.
Risk profile
A risk profile combines a person's ability and willingness to take risk, guiding the choice of investments.
An investor who cannot sleep after a small loss has a low willingness to take risk.
All investors have the same risk profile.
Asset allocation
Asset allocation divides investments among asset classes like equity, debt and gold, according to goals, horizon and risk profile.
A saver holds 60% equity, 30% debt and 10% gold.
Asset allocation means putting everything into one stock.
Time value of money
A rupee today is worth more than a rupee tomorrow because it can be invested to earn a return.
₹1 lakh invested today grows, so it is worth more than ₹1 lakh in five years.
Money has the same value at any time.
Compounding
Compounding means earning returns on both the original amount and the returns accumulated earlier, which accelerates growth over long periods.
Reinvested gains themselves earn further gains.
Compounding means earning returns only on the original amount.
Inflation
Inflation is the sustained rise in the general price level, reducing the purchasing power of money.
A basket of goods costing ₹100 last year costs ₹106 now.
Inflation raises the value of cash.
Emergency fund
An emergency fund is a reserve of liquid funds covering three to six months of expenses for unexpected needs.
A family keeps six months of expenses in a savings account.
An emergency fund should be invested in small-cap stocks.
Insurance and investment
Term insurance gives protection against loss of life; it should be separated from investment, which aims at building wealth.
A person buys a term plan for cover and invests separately for growth.
A mutual fund gives life cover.
Life-cycle stages
Different stages of life, such as starting a career, family and retirement, change goals, income and the right mix of assets.
A 25-year-old can usually hold more equity than a 60-year-old.
Life stage has no bearing on investments.
Diversification
Diversification spreads money across assets and securities to reduce the impact of any one loss.
An investor holds many companies across sectors instead of one.
Diversification guarantees no loss.
Investor grievance redressal
Investors can complain first to the intermediary, then to the exchange or SEBI's SCORES platform, and use the online dispute resolution route.
A client with an unresolved complaint files it on the regulator's portal.
Investors have no route for complaints.
Ponzi scheme
A Ponzi scheme pays earlier investors with the money of newer ones and promises unusually high, assured returns, and it collapses when new money dries up.
A scheme promises 4% a month and pays old investors from new deposits.
A scheme promising very high assured returns is safe.
Red flags in advice
Promises of guaranteed returns, pressure to invest quickly and unregistered advisers are warning signs of fraud.
A caller promises double returns in three months and asks for urgent payment.
Registered advisers promise assured returns.
Registered intermediary
Investors should deal only with SEBI-registered brokers, advisers and distributors, whose registration can be checked on the regulator's site.
An investor checks an adviser's registration number before engaging.
Registration of intermediaries is unnecessary.
Tax on investments
Tax treatment differs across securities and holding periods, so after-tax returns matter in planning.
Two investments with the same gain leave different amounts after tax.
All gains are taxed in the same way.
